CJP thinks they can turn India into Bangladesh. They are wrong. But the attempt is worth understanding in detail.

CJP chief Abhijeet Dipke just told opposition parties to stop contesting elections because they are rigged. Read that carefully. If elections are genuinely rigged the solution should be fixing the electoral process. But CJP's solution is to boycott elections entirely.

So how does the government change then?

Through the streets. Exactly the way BNP used violent protests in Bangladesh to overturn a government rather than winning through the ballot box. The template is not subtle. And the country recognises it.

But there are questions CJP never answers.

When Punjab had a paper leak under Congress, CJP was silent. When Jharkhand had a leak, CJP was silent. But when anything happens under BJP the protests are instant. EVM problems only appear when BJP wins. When the opposition won Punjab and Himachal the EVMs were apparently working perfectly.

That is not consistency. That is selective outrage designed to serve a specific agenda.

Then there is the funding question nobody in mainstream media is asking.

36 days of protests at Jantar Mantar. Stage, logistics, sound systems, crowd management, media coordination. None of that is free. Who paid for it?

CJP's co-convenor Saurav Das lives in a GK-1 luxury apartment at 9 to 10 lakh rupees per month in rent. For an NGO worker that money has to come from somewhere. Where exactly?

The organisation demanding maximum transparency from the government offers zero transparency about its own funding sources.

Now look at the timing.

When India refused to bend its independent foreign policy under American pressure, attempts to destabilise Indian institutions intensified almost immediately. The judiciary, the election commission, the military. Every institution that holds the country together became a simultaneous target.

Everyone saw what happened in Bangladesh.

The same script is being run in India.

The only difference is that this time people are watching.

To this day, I still don't understand why the 
government compromised with the CJP, why 
Dharmendra Pradhan resigned, and why the Prime 
Minister forgave those who abused the Prime Minister 
of India in front of the entire nation at Jantar Mantar.

I don't understand who Narendra Modi was to forgive 
them. Because the abuses at Jantar Mantar weren't 
directed at Narendra Modi, they were directed at the 
Prime Minister of this country. And whatever law exists 
for such indecency against the Prime Minister of the 
country, the law of the land was doing its job.

Who was Narendra Modi to interfere?

And the PM made four reels, garnering millions of 
views.
What was achieved by that?
Gen-Z wasn't abusive before, and they aren't abusive 
today either. The true Gen Z of the country thinks 
about the country, their career, their family, and their 
elders.

The people who abused at Jantar Mantar were not 
Gen Z. They were children far from home, uncontrolled 
by their parents, whose reformation is crucial when 
the stick is used.

Well, the CJP, whose stature was raised by the 
government, has no public support, no people with 
them; their stature grew only because of the 
government.

Today, they are visiting schools in every BJP-ruled 
state, demanding everyone's resignation and 
spreading anarchy. And now they are giving ultimatum to the country's Chief Election Commissioner with 
forty-eight hours to resign.
Wow! What a thing!

Does this mean there's so much freedom in this 
country that any random person can come and 
demand the resignation of any senior official of the 
country and give him a warning?
That's amazing.

And the biggest thing I don't understand is that four 
cockroaches sit down and make some 
announcements in the name of a press conference, 
and the microphones of the entire media of the 
country are in front of them.
Why? For What? Any Legitimity ???
Are they some big leaders?
Do they have a large following?
Or are they some big officers?
Or are they some legal experts?
A scholar?
An intellectual?
What is that?
Why does the media want to make the people of the 
country listen to them?

And just two days ago, in the same Delhi, some Gen-Z 
chapari type boys and girls hurled such filthy abuses 
at Modi and waved such filthy posters.
This videos are viral on Twitter. I can't write here about 
the abuses they (maily girls) hurled. I don't know what 
they were saying, but they were saying that Modi's is 
small, this is that.
In a way, I don't know about Modi, but this 
government's is definitely small....bamboo.
Because if the bamboo were big, Narendra Modi 
would never have intervened and forgiven the abusers 
at Jantar Mantar, and would have let the law do its 
work.
If this government's bamboo had any power, the 
government's bamboo would have been protruding 
from the throats of these abusers.
And we are not ignorant.
How much power the government's bamboo has, 
Kejriwal's police showed us, Uddhav Thackeray's 
police showed us, and their police in Karnataka, 
Kerala, and wherever Congress governments are in 
power, have also shown us.
We know how powerful the government's bamboo is, 
but we also know that the central government's 
bamboo doesn't have that power, or they're not using 
it.
Political existence doesn't survive solely on 
compulsion or chessboard. The public will be 
disgusted.

FOUR UPRISINGS — ONE COMMON QUESTION: WHO WILL BE ACCOUNTABLE?

https://t.co/nGeXul803i

AJIT SAHI ON A COUNTRY THAT IS BEGINNING TO QUESTION POWER

What happens when citizens in different parts of society begin saying the same thing in different languages?

Enough. We want answers.

In this conversation with Niddhesh Tyagi, journalist Ajit Sahi looks at the emerging wave of public dissent and argues that the Jantar Mantar mobilisation should not be viewed in isolation.

His larger argument is about a society where questions around education, employment, democratic institutions, accountability and political power are increasingly entering public consciousness.

And perhaps the most important point is this:

A democracy does not become stronger because citizens stop protesting.
It becomes stronger when citizens are free to question those who govern them.

The Jantar Mantar movement has demonstrated the importance of sustained civic pressure. Reporting from the period documented the continuing protest there and the participation of public figures and civil-society voices.

But protest alone is not democracy.

The real democratic test is whether institutions listen, explain, correct and remain accountable.

That is why every movement must ultimately return to the same constitutional questions:

Who is responsible?
What went wrong?
What evidence exists?
Who will answer?
And what changes will prevent it from happening again?

When citizens begin asking these questions without fear, something important happens.

Power discovers that it is being watched.

And when power is watched, questioned and constitutionally challenged, democracy is not weakened.

It is exercised.

The message from this conversation is therefore worth hearing:

Don't normalise silence.
Don't surrender your questions.
Don't confuse authority with accountability.

A democracy belongs neither to a government nor to an opposition.

It belongs to its citizens.

body:
How Modi Managed “THE MEDIA” To Stay In Power

In 2002, Gujarat CM Narendra Modi sat in front of a BBC camera and admitted his one real weakness:
“One area where I was very, very weak… that was how to handle the media.”

He never forgot that lesson. He just decided the media should never be allowed to become a problem again.
Fast forward to 2026.
Between March and July, the government sent one blocking order every 68 seconds to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube.

1.95 lakh orders in five months.
1,275 every single day.
Instagram — the platform students used during the Jantar Mantar protests — received more than 1 lakh of them.
Last year the daily average was six.

This is not “managing” the media.
This is industrial-scale silencing.

The same playbook that started with ED and CBI cases against NDTV, the takeover of Network18, and UAPA against NewsClick’s founder is now running on autopilot through the Sahyog portal. Content vanishes in three hours. Often without anyone even seeing the order.

A government that needs to issue a takedown every 68 seconds is not confident.
It is terrified of what people will say when they are not being watched.

That is how you stay in power for this long — not by answering questions, but by making sure the questions never reach the public.

When dissent is treated as a security threat and protest as a crime, the media is no longer a watchdog. It is just another department to be controlled.
The 2002 admission was honest.

The 2026 response is the real story. 68 seconds.
That’s how long this government takes to silence you.
He admitted one weakness in 2002. He spent the next 24 years making sure it never happened again.

WHEN THE VOTER BECOMES THE SUSPECT, DEMOCRACY IS IN DANGER

The most fundamental rule of democracy is brutally simple:

Citizens choose their government.
The government does not choose its citizens.

Yogendra Yadav's message goes to the heart of the present SIR controversy.

The question is not merely about an electoral form, a database or an administrative exercise.

It is about who controls the conditions under which a citizen can exercise the right to vote.

The recent confrontation at Jantar Mantar has added another dimension. More than 60 people, including Yogendra Yadav, Prashant Bhushan and student leader Neha Bora, were detained on September 25 while protesting over SIR and demanding accountability from the Election Commission. Police said the gathering did not have the required permission.

Now civil-society groups have submitted an intimation for another protest on October 2, Gandhi Jayanti. As of September 30, Delhi Police had not granted permission for the proposed gathering.

This creates a democratic question that deserves an answer:

If citizens cannot peacefully question the institution responsible for maintaining the electoral roll, where are they supposed to take their concerns?

Electoral rolls are not ordinary government records.

They determine who gets to participate in choosing the government.

That is why every deletion, every procedural change and every objection raised about the process deserves transparency, documentation and an effective opportunity for correction.

The Election Commission has defended the legality of its SIR decisions and rejected the suggestion of an institutional breakdown. That makes transparency even more important: the public deserves evidence, explanations and accessible records — not merely competing political claims.

Democracy cannot mean:

“Trust the institution and stay silent.”

Democracy means:

Question. Verify. Protest peacefully. Demand answers. Defend the constitutional right to participate.

Because the ballot is not a privilege handed down by those in power.

It is the citizen's voice.

And when that voice is threatened, democracy demands vigilance.

THE VOTER MUST CHOOSE THE GOVERNMENT — NEVER THE OTHER WAY AROUND.

PRASHANT BHUSHAN: “POLICE SERVES THE LAW — NOT THE RULING PARTY”

At a press conference, senior advocate Prashant Bhushan raised a fundamental democratic question:

Is the police accountable to the government of the day—or to the Constitution and the law?

In the supplied video, Bhushan refers to the Supreme Court’s 2006 Prakash Singh judgment, which addressed the need to insulate policing from undue political influence and laid down directions concerning police administration.

He argues that police should not enforce an order merely because it comes from the government if that order is unlawful. He also makes an explicit distinction between resisting state action and resorting to violence, saying citizens should not engage in violence even if confronted by police action.

His wider argument concerns the ongoing dispute over the Election Commission, electoral-roll revision and SIR.

On September 30, Bhushan joined Neha Bora and RJD MP Manoj Jha in announcing a proposed October 2, 11 AM gathering at Jantar Mantar, raising concerns about the Election Commission and electoral rolls.

Delhi Police had not granted permission as of September 30, according to reports, while organisers said they had submitted an intimation.

Whatever one's political position, the underlying constitutional questions deserve public scrutiny:

Who controls the police?
Who protects the citizen's right to dissent?
And what happens when institutions meant to protect constitutional rights become the subject of those very rights?

A democracy does not require citizens to agree with every protest.

It requires that lawful dissent can exist without fear—and that institutions remain accountable to the Constitution.

Question power.
Demand evidence.
Protect democratic rights.
Keep protest peaceful.

𝗔𝗿𝗲 𝗦𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗙𝗮𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝗕𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗥𝗲𝗴𝘂𝗹𝗮𝗿𝘀 𝗔𝘁 𝗘𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁?

𝗔 𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀

Journalist Mrityunjay Chaubey has questioned what he describes as the repeated presence of certain left-leaning activists at demonstrations involving very different issues. His comment comes amid a series of recent student and political protests in Delhi and Jharkhand.

“There are certain leftist faces that we see in almost all protests,” Chaubey said, asking whether protesting has effectively become their “full-time job.”

𝗝𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘀𝗮𝘄 𝘄𝗲𝗲𝗸𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝘀

Jharkhand recently witnessed major demonstrations by job aspirants over alleged irregularities in recruitment examinations. The agitation continued for weeks, and the state government eventually agreed to cancel three examinations after talks with student representatives. 

Later, the BJP also organised demonstrations across the state demanding withdrawal of cases against protesting students and a CBI investigation into alleged recruitment-exam irregularities. 

𝗘𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗶𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝘀

Delhi has now seen demonstrations against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. AISA organised a protest at Jantar Mantar, while NSUI activists separately demonstrated over concerns surrounding electoral rolls and the Election Commission's functioning. 

𝗕𝘂𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀𝗻’𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝘆𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁

Chaubey’s broader criticism raises a legitimate subject for public debate: why do some activists participate in numerous, unrelated demonstrations?

However, there is no verified evidence in the sources reviewed that recurring protesters are being paid simply to attend these demonstrations or to create chaos. Such a claim would require evidence rather than inference from someone appearing at multiple protests.

𝗔𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗶𝘀𝗺 𝗼𝗿 𝗳𝘂𝗹𝗹-𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴?

Some activists see regular participation in protests as part of political organising and democratic engagement. Critics, however, may question whether repeated participation across unrelated causes reflects genuine issue-based activism.

Ultimately, frequent participation can be documented, but motives should not be assumed without evidence.

THE E20 DEBATE: FACTS VS HYPOCRISY.
HERE'S AN UNDENIABLE FACT:
The E20 programme did not begin under the Modi government. Ethanol blending was approved years earlier, during the UPA. The difference is in execution. Blending remained stuck at roughly 1–1.5% for years before accelerating significantly under the NDA.
So, let's first get the politics out of the way.
If ethanol blending was acceptable in principle then, why is it suddenly portrayed as anti-people now?
Now, let's look at the arguments being presented by critics:
CRITICS ARGUMENT 1: E20 FUEL IS BEING PUSHED BY NDA TO KEEP SUGAR CANE FARMERS HAPPY.
There's no doubt Ethanol is creating an additional income stream for sugarcane farmers.
But governments have always handed out subsidies or incentives to farmers.
+ MSP exists for 23 crops. Sugar cane farmers get SAP or State Advised Price.
+ Fertiliser subsidies.
+ Cheap or free electricity.
+ Irrigation subsidies.
+ Procurement policies.
If these benefits to farmers are accepted as legitimate public policy, why is E20 policy being targeted in isolation for market distortion?
CRITICS ARGUMENT 2: ETHANOL PRODUCTION IS WATER CONSUMING.
Yes, sugarcane consumes a great deal of water.
But so do
+ Paddy cultivators. Just look at the tumbling water tables in Punjab, Haryana.
+ AI and data centers.
+ Semiconductor manufacturing.
+ Steel and cement production.
The question is not whether something uses water, but whether the benefits justify the costs. Again why are critics holding E20 alone to a test that they don't set for others?
CRITICS ARGUMENT 3: THE GOVERNMENT SHOULD NOT MAKE E20 MANDATORY. LEAVE IT TO CHOICE. 
We're in a democracy and choice matters. But governments routinely make decisions that we, the people have no choice but to accept.
+ Taxation rates
+ Emission norms.
+ Fuel quality standards.
+ Safety regulations.
+ Identity Proof.
These are often choices imposed to achieve broader national goals. Shouldn't E20 should be judged in the same way?
Here's how E20 usage serves NATIONAL INTEREST:
+ India imports 85–90% of its crude oil. E20 seeks to address that by replacing up to 20% of petrol volume with domestically produced ethanol, helping diversify the fuel mix and reducing import costs.
+ With E20 NDA estimates saving Rs 1 lakh crore in foreign-exchange.
CRITICS ARGUMENT 4: COST OF CAR ENGINE WEAR AND TEAR, MILEAGE INEFFICIENCY OUTWEIGHS BENEFITS.
It is true that Ethanol has about 34% less energy per litre than petrol. But because E20 contains only 20% ethanol, the overall energy content of the fuel falls by roughly 4%–7%. So at 5% a car that gives 20 km/L on pure petrol will give 19km/L. But usage also improves air quality. Which increases longevity in humans and lowers healthcare costs over time. That is s fair trade-off. 
CONCLUSION:
Every policy is a trade off. E20 isn't perfect. But if agricultural subsidies, procurement, irrigation policy and fuel regulations are accepted as legitimate public policy, then judge ethanol using the same yardstick.

body:
I am a practicing tax professional in India. For years I was a vocal supporter of this government. 

I defended it during various protests like CJP at jantar mantar and many others,  argued with friends and family and whoever questioned  @BJP4India 

I write this with pain, not anger but with a sense of betrayal. 

On 1 July 2017, at the ICAI Foundation Day, PM Modi told Chartered Accountants that their signature is more powerful than that of a Prime Minister, that the government trusts what CAs certify, and that we are ambassadors of the economic system. Today is 27 September 2026. The tax audit deadline is 30 September,  three days away. 

Over 40 representations from CA associations across India have gone to the Finance Minister and CBDT asking for a one-month extension to 31 October. The response has been complete silence. Not one official acknowledgment. Not even a tweet from @IncomeTaxIndia. 

On 22 September the department instead sent SMS reminders restating 30 September, as if those representations had never been filed.

This extension is not a luxury. It is a necessity created by the government’s own calendar.

 ITR-3 was released on 18 June, ITR-5 on 7 July, ITR-7 on 9 July and ITR-6 on 4 August 2026; the online utilities came even later. The non-audit ITR deadline was shifted to 31 August, so audit season began the next day, effectively 30 days for GST reconciliation, TDS matching, AIS/TIS cross-checks, MSME disclosures and 44AB reporting. ICAI’s new detailed financial statement format for non-corporate entities added more work in the same window. The e-filing portal’s peak season outages are on record, including the 26 July 2026 breakdown before the 31 July ITR deadline, Lok Sabha Unstarred Question No. 60 and the Ministry’s own reply admitted Infosys penalties for SLA breaches. 

A proposed bank strike on 28–30 September, after the fourth-Saturday holiday and Sunday, threatens to shut branch banking for five straight days in the last compliance window. AY 2026-27 is also a transition year: the Income-tax Act, 1961 still governs the assessment year, while the Income-tax Act, 2025 is already in force from 1 April 2026. 

Last year CBDT extended the audit deadline from 30 September to 31 October and then to 10 November, with the ITR date to 10 December, by Circular No. 15/2025. The precedent exists. The case this year is stronger. Rajasthan Tax Consultants Association has already gone to the Rajasthan High Court (CW/54522/2026); the next hearing is 28 September. 

@theicai which is supposed to speak for four lakh CAs, has publicly hesitated to seek an extension “without a compelling reason,” even as industry feedback shows most pending audits still far from complete.

Tax professionals are not asking for favours. We are asking for working infrastructure, a workable timeline, and the dignity of a reply. We file the returns that fund the Union. We reconcile data the systems still cannot process cleanly.

 If CA signatures truly carry “immense faith,” forty plus signed representations should have produced at least an acknowledgment. 

The Finance Minister told an international tax conference in Bengaluru on 16 September fourteen days before this deadline that the philosophy is to make voluntary compliance easier. Then acknowledge the representations. Extend the tax audit deadline. Fix the portal. And stop confusing conference lines with ground reality.

And if this government wants the professional middle class still listening in 2029, start by replacing indifference with a reply extend the date, fix the portal, and stop delivering simplification speeches while the people who implement the law are ignored.

WHEN THE ELECTION COMMISSION ITSELF IS UNDER QUESTION

https://t.co/8MLxqS84oz

THE QUESTIONS ARE NO LONGER COMING ONLY FROM THE OPPOSITION.

The Indian Express investigation reported that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi recorded objections at least 14 times in 10 months over decisions relating to electoral rolls, SIR and the Commission's IT systems. 

Now the controversy has moved beyond the walls of the Election Commission.

CEC Gyanesh Kumar's youth-awareness programmes in Meerut and Varanasi were postponed. The ECI says the postponements were routine and unrelated to the internal controversy, citing logistical and scheduling reasons. 

At the same time, NDA ally Chirag Paswan publicly said that if questions are being raised about the Election Commission, the Commission must answer the public and remove doubts about the electoral process. 

And on September 25, Delhi Police dispersed protesters at Jantar Mantar; Newslaundry reported that journalist Irfan Ahmed was detained and that his microphone was allegedly snatched and thrown away. 

This is the point where every democrat should stop and ask:

Why is there so much institutional controversy around something as fundamental as the electoral roll?

We don't need conspiracy theories.
We don't need unverified accusations.
We need records, explanations, transparency and accountability.

If objections were formally recorded, answer them.
If the objections were resolved, publish how.
If the electoral database is functioning properly, make its safeguards transparent.
If programmes were postponed for ordinary reasons, explain those reasons clearly.

Because the legitimacy of every elected government ultimately rests on one simple principle:

The citizen must be able to trust that their vote exists, is counted, and cannot be arbitrarily denied.

Democracy survives not when citizens blindly trust institutions —
but when institutions are strong enough to withstand scrutiny.

body:
Today's Mint Long Story by @sayantanbera lays bare India's graduate employment crisis:
A physics teacher in a government school in Delhi got a call last month. His former student, Yashvardhan Kumar Mishra, was on the other end. Mishra had scored 92% in his boards, then 99 percentile in NEET. Good enough for a seat in a private medical college. Not good enough to afford it. The family had already spent over ₹10 lakh on coaching. His elder sibling has a computer science degree from a private college and has been looking for work in Delhi for four years. So Mishra let go of the medical seat. He considered nursing. His old teacher talked him out of it, told him he was too bright for that. He is now preparing to sit NEET again in 2026-27. His second drop year.

The promise was simple. Study hard, move up. That promise is coming apart in the data too. 39% of graduates under 25 were unemployed in 2023. Worse than 1983, when it was 35%. Annual earnings for male graduates aged 20-29 fell 0.8% between 2011 and 2017. They had grown 3.4% in the seven years before that.
A poster at the Jantar Mantar protest site put it plainly: education was supposed to be for all, it has become for the rich only.

body:
November 7, 1966. ~125,000 people came to Delhi to demand a national ban on cow slaughter. Naga sadhus and ascetics led the march. It went from Jantar Mantar to Parliament.

Police fired on it. The official death toll was 7. Hindu organisations have put the figure far higher and said that bodies were removed overnight. No inquiry ever settled the question, which is itself the point.

Gulzarilal Nanda was Home Minister. His own party made him resign on November 9 and Yashwantrao Chavan replaced him.

Indira Gandhy then constituted a committee to examine a national law banning cow slaughter and put M.S. Golwalkar on it. The committee sat for years. No law came out of it.

A government fired on sadhus outside Parliament, then set up a committee to keep the question warm until the country forgot the shooting.

body:
An Open Letter to the Jantar Mantar protestors:

My dear young friends,

I address you today not as a politician or an MP, but as someone deeply troubled by what is happening to your generation of young Indians.

This is personal for me. I was born to a middle-class family: my father was a salaried newspaper employee, my mother a homemaker, with three children to educate on one income. For a family like ours, merit was not a slogan. Scholarships, fair examinations, honest results — these were the only way one salary could carry three children's dreams. 

I went to school in Mumbai and Kolkata, to college here in Delhi, topped the University and earned admission into IIM — and chose instead to follow my passion for international affairs, in America, on a scholarship. Nothing was inherited; everything was earned by hard work and yes, Exams.

So I know that a fair, merit-based system is the only ladder for young people from lower and middle-income families to climb up. When that ladder is broken — papers leaked, examinations cancelled, trust destroyed — the children of the rich and powerful do not suffer. They have other ladders. It is your dreams, and your families' sacrifices (and tragically, in some homes, young lives themselves) that are betrayed.

To the young people gathered at Jantar Mantar, and those raising your voices peacefully across India: this country hears you. Your anger is not indiscipline — it is the anguish of a generation that did everything right and was still betrayed . You are not alone.

And to the millions of young Indians watching quietly: your generation is not a problem to be managed. You are the answer to India's future. Do not lose hope. This ladder will be rebuilt — by you, and by every Indian who stands with you.

To Shri Sonam Wangchuk-ji, my heartfelt appeal: please end your fast. You have awakened the conscience of the nation;  that is what a fast is meant to do. India needs your voice for the long road ahead. 

With Parliament in session again from Monday, we will have an opportunity to raise the students’ issues in the highest forum of our democracy. That’s where the problem should be addressed, not by fasting unto death. Please heed my plea. 

And finally, to the Government:  I respectfully urge you to reach out and engage in the dialogue our democracy owes its young citizens. That is not weakness; that is statesmanship.

Jantar Mantar already showed the method.

When the lathi charge came, the big faces were not in the crush.

Gen Z is expected to absorb the baton.

Home Buyers created storm at Jantar Mantar against decade-Long Red Tape Struggle for Metro, Registry and possession of flats.

Thousands of Home Buyers from Greater Noida west reached jantar mantar using multiple Buses from many societies to protest and raise their demand heard for Metro, Registry, Possession of flats and random wierd decisions by IRP.

The ambitious Aqua Metro extension project to Greater Noida West, spearheaded by the NOIDA Metro Rail Corporation (NMRC), has been entangled in bureaucratic red tape for over a decade. Despite the initial preparation of a detailed project report (DPR) by DMRC, state government approval, and endorsement by the Public Investment Board (PIB) of the central government, the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) has recently rejected the proposal, leaving the fate of the project uncertain.

The situation has raised questions about the numerous hurdles the project must overcome and how many more years it will take to see completion. Despite the recommendations from the Amitabh Kant Committee aimed at resolving issues related to registry and possession, the authorities appear nonchalant, leaving thousands of homebuyers in limbo.

Efforts to find a resolution have been ongoing for decades, with multiple meetings, continuous agitation, and a year-long protest at Ek Murti Chowk yielding no positive results. The recent gathering of thousands of buyers from various societies in Greater Noida West at Jantar Mantar underscores the urgency of their demand to kick-start metro construction in the area.

The protest, led by the NEFOWA, aims to draw attention to the need for immediate action on the Amitabh Kant Committee report. The report suggests expediting the registry of flats and completing stalled projects to address the concerns of frustrated homebuyers.

Abhishek Kumar, President of NEFOWA, expressed frustration, stating, "The protest will continue to intensify as we witness one approval after another, followed by sudden rejections for the metro project."

Mihir Gautam, Convener of the Registry and Possession Movement, lamented the apparent disconnect between the government and the plight of homebuyers, saying, "It is hard to believe that such a popular government is unable to understand the plight of lakhs of homebuyers who are being extorted by authorities and builders."

The rally at Jantar Mantar is a plea for urgent action from both the State and Central governments to fulfill this long-standing demand for a metro extension in Greater Noida West. The citizens hope that their collectie voice will finally bring about the serious efforts required to resolve the persisting issues.

- "Since Gyanesh Kumar became the CEC, the 𝗴𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗯𝗲 𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝘃𝗼𝘁𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗻𝗼𝘁. Is this democracy? You have turned the entire concept of democracy upside down" (The Wire).

- "Is Gyanesh Kumar deleting them 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 to widen that 2% gap so that they never lose office?" Dipke asked (New Indian Express).

🗣️ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗪𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴
- "If within 48 hours Gyanesh Kumar doesn't resign, the CJP will start a 𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘄𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗮𝗴𝗶𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻. We won't step back till the time Gyanesh Kumar resigns" (Mathrubhumi).

- CJP cancelled all Thursday programmes and called the press conference on the "Hijacking of India's Democracy" at noon (The Hindu).
- Dipke was accompanied by co-conveners Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka (The Wire).
- "Chief Election Commissioner is the 𝗯𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶-𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹. Gyanesh Kumar is the 𝗯𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶-𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗿𝘆. He should resign immediately because he is the 𝗯𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗮'𝘀 𝗱𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗰𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘆," Dipke said (Mathrubhumi).
- "Since Gyanesh Kumar became the CEC, the 𝗴𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗯𝗲 𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝘃𝗼𝘁𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗻𝗼𝘁. Is this democracy? You have turned the entire concept of democracy upside down" (The Wire).

- "Is Gyanesh Kumar deleting them 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 to widen that 2% gap so that they never lose office?" Dipke asked (New Indian Express).

body:
Several protesters were detained in Delhi on Friday as a demonstration against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar unfolded amid heavy police restrictions.

The protest, organised by the All India Students’ Association (AISA) along with civil society groups, was announced by AISA president Neha Bora, with activists and public figures including Yogendra Yadav among those backing the call.

But protesters were stopped from entering the designated protest site at Jantar Mantar. Police told them they did not have permission to enter the area, following which several protesters were detained.

In an interview with The Quint, Bora spoke about the police action, the restrictions on the protest and why the groups are demanding accountability from the Election Commission.

The protest comes amid growing criticism of Kumar following reports about disagreements within the Election Commission over decisions linked to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.

- CJP cancelled all Thursday programmes and called the press conference on the "Hijacking of India's Democracy" at noon (The Hindu).
- Dipke was accompanied by co-conveners Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka (The Wire).
- "Chief Election Commissioner is the 𝗯𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶-𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹. Gyanesh Kumar is the 𝗯𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶-𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗿𝘆. He should resign immediately because he is the 𝗯𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗮'𝘀 𝗱𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗰𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘆," Dipke said (Mathrubhumi).
- "Since Gyanesh Kumar became the CEC, the 𝗴𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗯𝗲 𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝘃𝗼𝘁𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗻𝗼𝘁. Is this democracy? You have turned the entire concept of democracy upside down" (The Wire).

- "Is Gyanesh Kumar deleting them 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 to widen that 2% gap so that they never lose office?" Dipke asked (New Indian Express).

- 𝗙𝗿𝗲𝗲𝘇𝗲 𝗦𝗜𝗥 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗵𝗼𝗹𝗱 𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀: All upcoming elections must be put on hold. The SIR must be frozen. The electoral roll must be 𝗿𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗱 𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗝𝗮𝗻𝘂𝗮𝗿𝘆 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟱 𝘃𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗹𝗶𝘀𝘁. An independent inquiry commission must be constituted (The Wire).
- 𝗥𝗲𝗽𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟯 𝗹𝗮𝘄: The Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment) Act, 2023 must be repealed and replaced with new legislation with civil society participation (Times Now).
- All files linked to the SIR must be placed in the 𝗰𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗱𝘆 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝘂𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘁 to prevent records from disappearing (NDTV).

🗣️ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗪𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴
- "If within 48 hours Gyanesh Kumar doesn't resign, the CJP will start a 𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘄𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗮𝗴𝗶𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻. We won't step back till the time Gyanesh Kumar resigns" (Mathrubhumi).
- "If the CEC doesn't resign, 𝗝𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗿 𝗠𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗿 𝟮.𝟬 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗱𝗲𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗹𝘆 𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻" (Daily Pioneer).
- Dipke urged opposition parties: "You cannot participate in a contest you know is rigged while complaining about it on the sidelines. Taking part legitimises the outcome" (NDTV).
- The ECI responded that differing views are a normal part of deliberations and all decisions were unanimous (New Indian Express).

CJP has drawn its line. 𝗚𝘆𝗮𝗻𝗲𝘀𝗵 𝗞𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗿 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝟰𝟴 𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻. 𝗜𝗳 𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁, 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘆 𝗶𝗻 𝗗𝗲𝗹𝗵𝗶. 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗴𝗼 𝘁𝗼 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗲.

Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke addressed a press conference in Delhi on Thursday, issuing Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar a 𝟰𝟴-𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗺 to resign, warning of a nationwide agitation if he does not step down (NDTV, The Wire).

📰 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲
- CJP cancelled all Thursday programmes and called the press conference on the "Hijacking of India's Democracy" at noon (The Hindu).
- Dipke was accompanied by co-conveners Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka (The Wire).
- "Chief Election Commissioner is the 𝗯𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶-𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹. Gyanesh Kumar is the 𝗯𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶-𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗿𝘆. He should resign immediately because he is the 𝗯𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗮'𝘀 𝗱𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗰𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘆," Dipke said (Mathrubhumi).
- "Since Gyanesh Kumar became the CEC, the 𝗴𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗯𝗲 𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝘃𝗼𝘁𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗻𝗼𝘁. Is this democracy? You have turned the entire concept of democracy upside down" (The Wire).

- "Is Gyanesh Kumar deleting them 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 to widen that 2% gap so that they never lose office?" Dipke asked (New Indian Express).

🗣️ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗪𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴
- "If within 48 hours Gyanesh Kumar doesn't resign, the CJP will start a 𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘄𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗮𝗴𝗶𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻. We won't step back till the time Gyanesh Kumar resigns" (Mathrubhumi).

What they achieved in Jantar mantar is commendable sir.

Most important achievement is, that it restored the courage of people to question the Government and the facade of invincibility fell off from Modi and co.

That is no mean feat.

And as a substantial achievement the person under whose watch the NEET leak of 2024 and 2026 (most likely 2025 also, only that we didn't hear about it) happened had to go.

That they pulled off this feat despite all kind of choking by the Government, speaks volumes about their resolve and capability.  Once the Government conceded to all their stated demands there is little ground to prolong their protest without severe legal repercussions. There will be nobody to their support if they were incarcerated under some draconian provisions. Including you and me, who want positive changes to happen miraculously.

That they are taking up the cudgels again, again on a very important matter that concerns the country, in a combative way, under huge risks, is a testament to their integrity, resolve and capability.

I wish them well, will support in all ways that I can and I will hope that they will succeed.

Again.

body:
Why is BJP in defensive mode?

by Prabhu Chawla 

The reversal can be validated. A top judicial functionary likening unemployed young activists to cockroaches became, almost overnight, a name, a costume and a crowd.

Ignorance, the old line goes, is bliss. Bliss turns to blisters when ignorance is the only reply to a threat nobody has troubled to understand. That is the weather over Indian politics now. For the first time in 12 years of power, the Bharatiya Janata Party is answering more than it is asking. A jeering youth revolt, a quarrel over the Election Commission and a campaign against squalid village schools have pushed a party that once wrote the terms of debate into the unfamiliar business of explanation.

The BJP’s long advantage was never simply the vote. It was command of the argument. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s popularity, a complete compendium of welfare and development medals, and his mighty machine faster than any rival’s facilitated the BJP decide what the country discussed. Around it grew a climate of sympathetic television, retired officials offering public praise, fading celebrities discovering sudden conviction and corporate voices that changed colour with the occupant of power. Criticism existed, but rarely set the terms.

That mechanism wasn’t built for post-2014 India. Unlike the voters who rode the first Modi wave, the first-time voters today are driven by memes and algorithms; they have scant patience for sermons about Nehru or the pedigree of an expressway. They do not reject the past as much as they refuse to be moved by it either. Praise for the new dispensation, that once travelled as energy, has frozen.

The reversal can be validated. A top judicial functionary likening unemployed young activists to cockroaches became, almost overnight, a name, a costume and a crowd. The Cockroach Janta Party began as a satire and then walked onto the street. The trigger was a leaked medical entrance test and the demand that the Union education minister resign.

But the ammunition like an examination system that felt purchasable and a job market unable to absorb the graduates it certified. Satire achieved what conventional opposition briefings had not, turning an insult into a uniform and marching it to Jantar Mantar.

The party’s first response was predictable one. For the BJP, the movement was a meme, a proxy, a passing pest. It still believed that the dialect worked against a dynastic opponent with a familiar surname. In reality, it died against students in insect masks quoting the Constitution and filming a classroom without a roof. Only after a protest camp, a hunger strike, a march on Parliament dispersed with tear gas and a Congress demonstration outside the Prime Minister’s residence did the government change course.

Talks, a resignation, a tougher law on paper leaks and a purge at the testing agency followed. These were concessions extracted by pressure, not a communications triumph. Perhaps, during the past 12 years the party just forgot to encourage constructive and corrective disagreement to deal with the mobile-driven motivated crowd. Now its own allies are questioning the abominable demeanour of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, a major source of embarrassment for the ruling party.

A handful of ministers can still fight on this terrain. They occasionally concede a fact before disputing a motive. The party’s public faces just cannot. Too many spokespersons are late arrivals from other parties or from TV studios, who know how to shout. But fail to offer a logical counterpoint. Personal ridicule does not answer a 19-year-old who couldn’t appear in a competitive exam.

Nor does a charge of bad faith answer draft electoral rolls from which a vast numbers of names have vanished, while reports of dissent within the commission itself spill into the open. The commission calls the revision hygiene; much of the young public hears an umpire leaning towards the government. Rather than looking at the system passionately, the BJP is defending the referee when it once chose the sport.

The leadership has been slow to grasp this perceptive shift. For over 10 years, the charge against Rahul Gandhi was that he was not enough. The generation behind the CJP, with Congress hurrying to stand where the cameras already point has changed the indictment. Perhaps the BJP hadn’t geared itself to effectively win the battles of perception.

The argument now concerns the institutions meant to guard the vote, the exam, the school and the promise of work. When those fail, young voters hear not a debate about 1955 or 1975, but serious damage done to the institutions that were supposed to give them a fair chance. Young India needs to know who will stand for a clean examination, a safe school, work that is more than a slogan, and an Election Commission that looks independent even to those who voted against the government.

The party already holds a stronger favourable narrative than the one it deploys. Twenty-five years of the Prime Minister’s Executive life can be offered as unfinished service by a leader who will be judged by the next decade rather than embalmed by the last. Weak defence of a disreputable commission, a failing delivery system, a sycophantic bureaucracy and turncoats would only amplify the opposition’s noise. Such defence thrills a studio, but never reassures a young voter who suspects those who are demolishing institutions to retain their plum posts.

The BJP can still win the war after losing small battles. It can’t be won through the imported spokesperson, but through the ideological foot-soldier. The BJP’s historic gift was the worker who knew the lane, the booth, the grievance and the face behind it. The cadre must set the environment and stop the leadership from asking the booth-worker to defend at a tea stall what cannot be defended in public. While in opposition, the BJP never waited to be handed an agenda. It turned inflation, graft and captured institutions into short public debate and forced the government to yield. Now the power has made it forget the craft. But the craft can be reclaimed without nostalgia or surrender.

Rahul and the CJP did not invent this anger. They have simply been quicker to occupy the ground created by dissatisfaction. The BJP’s trouble is not a shortage of talent to invoke, but that invocation has replaced listening. Its loudspeakers still work; they no longer decide the pitch. Bliss, in politics, is the luxury of not learning. The BJP needs to adopt the humility to hear contrarian voices from within. The party can still seize the initiative on delivery, on reform and on institutions that look like institutions. If it chooses accusatory rebuttal alone, the blisters will teach the rest.

परफ़ॉर्मेटिव हिन्दुत्वा बनाम हिन्दुत्व

भाजपा वालों को अब बहुत परिश्रम करना पड़ रहा है 'हिंदू' दिखने के लिए। 'चक्षु दान' से झुनझुने वाली डफली तक, जो पहले सामान्य लगता था, अपेक्षित लगता था, अब एक परफॉरमेंस लगता है। आप ब्रह्मा को गाली देने वाले फुले और 22 प्रतिज्ञाओं वाले अम्बेडकर को, भगवान राम और शिव के साथ कैसे प्रमोट कर सकते हैं! 

अब त्रिपुंड, त्रिशूल और भगवा केवल तब दिखता है जब आलोचना हो, जब आपकी विभाजनकारी नीतियों को समाज पकड़ कर, आपसे उत्तर माँगने लगा हो। अब, न तो आप ‘पाइड पाइपर ऑफ हैमलिन’ हैं, न ही हिन्दू समाज चूहों की तरह तुम्हारी ‘पेन्ही नीली सरिया ए मेहरिया, जै भीम बोला’ धुन सुन कर पीछे चलने लगेगा। 

इनकी धृष्टता देखो कि एक घोषित जातिवादी, विभाजनकारी, हिन्दू समाज भंजक नेता के जन्मदिन पर ये लोग ‘दीप जलाओ’ का कार्यक्रम ऐसे कर रहे थे, जैसे भगवान राम का अयोध्या आगमन हो रहा हो! पूर्ण निर्लज्जता के साथ!

और यह जीव इस बकलोली को ‘न’ भी नहीं बोल पा रहा। दिखास, छपास और आत्ममुग्धता के चरम पर बैठे इस व्यक्ति की टीम को इनके छवि प्रबंधन में अब भगवान बना कर, अगले कुछ वर्षों में भगवान से भी ऊपर बताने की योजना है कि राम-नाम तो कुछ नहीं हैं। अब बनारस में देव दीपावली से बड़ा आयोजन ‘नमो दीपावली’ होनी चाहिए। इन फैक्ट, इनका वश चले तो बनारस का नाम ‘नमोरस’ करवा दें! 

अब ये गिनीज बुक ऑफ वर्ल्ड रिकॉर्ड्स में समाहित होना चाहते हैं कि ब्रो इतने दीये जल गए सर के नाम से! पहले यह रिकॉर्ड अयोध्या के राम जी के नाम था। इनका हिन्दुत्व केवल और केवल मार्केटिंग तकनीक बन कर बच गया है, जहाँ काम खत्म होते ही हिन्दू प्रतीक केवल एक प्रॉप बन कर रह जाता है। 

इनका हर कार्य एक आयोजन है। इनका हर आयोजन एक स्पेक्टेकल है। हर स्पेक्टेकल एक स्टेज है इनकी विजिबिलिटी के लिए। हर विजिबिलिटी एक्सरसाइज एक वेल-क्राफ्टेड स्ट्रेटेजी है किसी ऐसे लक्ष्य को पाने के लिए, जो ये अनिच्छा से करते हैं, पर राजनीति के लिए आवश्यक है। 

सवर्ण समाज अब इसे एक नौटंकी के रूप में देखता है। पहले आह्लादित हो कर हम पोस्ट लिखते थे, रील बनाते थे, बताते थे कि देखो हिन्दुओं को हिन्दू होना सिखाया! हम भी उलझते थे लोगों से कि तुम्हें समझ नहीं आ रहा, ये सब जरूरी है, सोए हिन्दुओं का आत्मविश्वास वापस ला रहा है। बात को समझो। 

अब हम बस अपने अधिकारों की बात करेंगे। हमारा हिन्दुत्व हम देख लेंगे, आप अपनी राजनीति खुल कर करो। अम्बेडकर को पूजो, हमें कोई समस्या नहीं। पर ये नौटंकी इसलिए मत करो कि हम मान लें कि नहीं यार, हिन्दुत्ववादी है।

CJP’s 48-hour ultimatum to CEC Gyanesh Kumar is not civic concern.

It is an open threat of street disruption dressed up as democracy.

A self-styled outfit with documented AAP fingerprints now demands the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, a freeze on the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, and a return to older lists because the cleanup of inflated and dubious entries threatens their politics.

That is not reform.

That is an attempt to hold the Election Commission hostage.​

Abhijeet Dipke and his circle have no constitutional authority to issue deadlines to a constitutional authority. 

The CEC is not a party worker.

He is not required to resign because a protest group, after an Indian Express report on internal notes, suddenly discovered “vote theft.” SIR is a lawful, periodic exercise to purify rolls.

If names were wrongly deleted, the remedy is claims, objections, and courts not Jantar Mantar 2.0 and nationwide chaos.​

The coincidence with Sonam Wangchuk’s remark is not subtle.

On the same stretch of days, Wangchuk claimed India’s governance in Ladakh is worse than China’s oppression in Tibet. 

The Central Tibetan Administration itself called that comparison misplaced and inaccurate.

Equating a Union Territory of the Indian Republic with Tibet under the CCP is not “activism.” 

It is a slur on the Indian state and an insult to every soldier and citizen who lives with the reality of that border.​

This is the pattern: one network manufactures a 48-hour crisis in Delhi; another face of earlier agitation supplies the anti India soundbite from the frontier.

Psychological pressure, urban disruption, and foreign-comparison rhetoric are then packaged as “public sentiment.”

It is a coordinated attempt to delegitimise institutions that stand between them and perpetual street veto.

The public is tired of this script.

The Election Commission must complete SIR without intimidation.

The government must stop treating organised disruption as sacred protest. 

Ultimatums to the CEC, threats of Jantar Mantar 2.0, and comparisons of India with China’s Tibet are not dissent.

They are a challenge to the constitutional order.

Meet them as such.

INDIA'S MID-POWER BARGAIN 

I believe Operation Sindoor tweaked something uncanny, that suddenly, much of India's geopolitics got fuzzy after that. Maybe it was the Air India crash that had something to do with it. Maybe it was Kirana Hills. Or maybe it was the complete deep cleansing of Maoist militancy that corroded the nation from deep within.

And then just to the near west, the Iran-Israel-US war blew up the global energy landscape, putting an arrow straight to the heart of an oil-dependent 1.5 billion people nation.

And now, a season later, a series of incidents that make South Block look like it's flinching. Jantar Mantar was handed over to an anarchist circus with foreign fingerprints all over it and nobody touching them, a US ambassador walking into Manipur, Western and Northern Command like he owns a security clearance. FCRA quietly slow-walked, MDR slapped onto UPI after Washington complained about it (okay, you call it narrative spinning, but narratives reign supreme), and finally the gut punch- an American mercenary and his full Ukrainian crew, caught destabilizing the Northeast, released and waved home.

The social verdict portrays that India blinked. The government is compromised. Modi's grip has slipped and the price is being paid in terrible optics, in sovereignty, in credibility. How should I read it? I search for the layers, the invisible ones. What does it indicate in the long trajectories of power?

A superpower doesn't need back channels. It dictates through front doors, and it kicks them in. If you observe New Delhi is trading, that says it all. It's a tell of realpolitik. It's the tell of exactly what India is at the moment: A mid-level power, sitting on 1.5 billion people who need energy, capital, and market access flowing in without interruption, in a time where the global energy stakeholders are actively bombing each other’s oil supply lines. Now, if you are at the helm of affairs, how would you keep one and a half billion people safe and thriving?

What did Kautilya map out of a similar situation, which a king may face in a mid-power situation? Sama, Dana, Danda, Bheda?  Wisdom doesn't pick one and commit for life. Rigidity doesn’t work, as Bruce Lee said to be like water. Wisdom reads the boardgame in each of the cases. Right now, with Washington, India is running Dana and Sama simultaneously, so that in the calculated future the Danda can be enforced where it is planned. This is difficult to digest, but that is how power works. 

India cannot overpower the United States or China, at this moment. Anyone building a thesis on the fantasy that New Delhi is secretly outmanoeuvring both is lying to you. That is not the game India is playing. What India is, practically, a mid-power- a nation with enough weight to matter at the table, but not enough weight to own the table. And a mid-power survives one way: by constantly trading something to protect something bigger, till it outgrows its counterparts. And certainly India cannot take the path of Israel or Iran, simply because that would be suicidal to put the lives of a billion people at stake. 

What does it get in return? Unhindered oil flows despite sanctions. A controlled neighbourhood to plan its next move. And an identity where, even amid war, both Tel Aviv and Tehran still call India a friend. A position where Moscow, Washington and Beijing need Delhi’s cooperation more than Delhi needs any one of them.

That is the actual trade. The thesis what I see is straightforward. Internal optics is being spent, to buy external security, currency protection and energy continuity for 1.5 billion people, while silently building the alternate energy production in nuclear, after decades of stagnancy.  

Call it weak if you only see the internal picture. But a mid-power that tries to look strong on every front eventually runs out of leverage where it matters. The real strength is choosing which game to lose publicly so it doesn’t lose the one it can’t afford to.

Yes, Andhra Pradesh is part of India—and precisely because it is, our responsibility is to put Andhra Pradesh first.

A regional party may not form the government at the Centre on its own, but it can still have independent political leverage by supporting or opposing legislation issue-by-issue.

body:
People supporting this are brain-dead lackeys, as usual, of govt.

Just ask yourself how will it be done?

Here's the ugly part nobody in power wants to say out loud: age verification at scale in India means Aadhaar verification. Full stop. One roundtable with lawyers, technologists, and platform reps concluded that any age check "robust enough to work risks developing into a persistent, Aadhaar-linked identity layer for every internet user, not just children". Not just kids. Everyone. To prove your 13-year-old is 13, every adult in the country gets pushed through a biometric gate to scroll. That's the "how."

And the legal premise they're using? Minors can't enter contracts under Section 11 of the Contract Act, so their accounts are "void ab initio". The Supreme Court is now asking the Centre to make 18 the minimum age for social media membership. Sounds clean on paper. It is not.

Here's what they're not telling you: this doesn't even work. Australia banned under-16s in December 2025. By July 2026, testers opened 50 accounts declaring the user as 16. Not one platform asked for proof of age. All 50 stayed active across nine of ten platforms. The eSafety Commissioner is now investigating Meta, YouTube, Snapchat and TikTok for non-compliance. You know what kids did instead? Drew beards on their faces to fool the facial scans. Used their parents' accounts. Spiked VPN usage by 1,800% in three days after the UK's Online Safety Act. India already has a 43% VPN adoption rate, the second-highest in the world. Every teenager in this country already knows how to route around this in five minutes.

And here's what the real cost looks like: Australia(among the first countries) is pushing platforms toward AI and biometric age estimation, facial geometry scans to prove you're old enough to exist online. Centralised biometric profiles of children. High-value honeypots of identity data waiting to be breached, subpoenaed or sold. One expert put it plainly: "I would not be very comfortable with a hardware company, any kind of company or government for that matter, running facial recognition on my child".

This isn't protection. It's a pipeline. And the infrastructure being built today for "child safety" doesn't go away tomorrow. Nikhil Pahwa from MediaNama said it best: social media is just the beginning. "I'm sure gaming and AI will be the first to be included after social media is. I see that as the first step in a longer direction of bringing age verification to everyone's usage of the internet".

But let's be real about the timing. Because this is also a way to suppress dissent.

This government is already deeply unpopular among Gen Z and young people. And they know it. Look at the numbers:

Unemployment among 15- to 29-year-olds rose to 16.2% in 2026, up from 13.8% the year before. India has the world's largest youth population, over 360 million people between 15 and 29, and the economy is failing them. Between 2004-05 and 2023, approximately five million graduates were added each year, but only around 2.8 million found employment. The labour market "has become brutal in the last 10 years". And the young know it. 

Then came the CJP... whatever your opinions of cjp is..but the fact is...

A youth-led, online-fuelled movement that started over exam paper leaks but exploded into something much bigger. Tens of thousands of students took to the streets of New Delhi. They forced the education minister to resign—a rare climbdown for a PM who spent a decade cultivating an image of unwavering resolve. 

And how did the government respond? By trying to silence them. As usual.

Between March and July 2026, the Centre issued nearly ~1.90 lakh blocking orders to social media platforms- that's one blocking order every 68 seconds. Around 1,275 every day. The period directly overlapped with the student protests. Over half of those orders went to Instagram, which had become the key organising platform for the movement. Meta integrated its API with the government's Sahyog portal, allowing content flagged by the government to be automatically taken down without any human review. No judge. No hearing. No appeal. Just an automated pipeline from the Home Ministry to your feed.

They also blocked the CJP's central domain and restricted its X handle. They suspended localised internet service around protest hubs, including Delhi's Jantar Mantar. India ranked second worldwide in internet shutdowns last year, according to Access Now. The authorities in Delhi used AI-powered camera technology to monitor and identify demonstrators. And women who attended the protests received rape threats and abusive messages after their videos went viral.

So here's the connection nobody in the mainstream media will make: the same government that is now building an age-verification wall around the internet just spent five months frantically trying to silence the largest youth protest movement in a decade. They saw what young people can do with social media. They saw a decentralised, leaderless movement force a cabinet resignation. And now they want to make sure it can't happen again. They are afraid of dissent.

The state has no business dictating what a child sees. That's a parent's job. A family's job. Not a bureaucrat's. Not a minister's. Not a Supreme Court bench's. The moment you accept "the government knows best what your kid should look at," you've already lost the argument. Because the same logic that bans Instagram for a 15-year-old today bans a protest hashtag for a 30-year-old tomorrow. The principle is identical: the state decides what information you're allowed to consume.

Every parent deserves to be worried about what their kid sees online. But the answer isn't a digital ID wall around the internet. The answer isn't handing the keys to a government that already runs the world's largest biometric ID system, a government that has shown, in real time, exactly what it does when young people use social media to hold it accountable.

The state has no business in your child's browser history. Full stop.

body:
Protect children first.

India is now considering a much stricter approach to minors on social media. On September 28, the Supreme Court asked the Centre to put statutory rules in place requiring social-media platforms to conform to Indian law, including an 18-year threshold for independent membership. 

The Solicitor General told the Court the government was ready to act. Under the Majority Act and Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, a person below 18 is not competent to independently enter a contract. The proposed 18+ restriction, however, has not yet become a final notified rule.

Australia shows why enforcement matters as much as the number written in the law. Its under-16 restrictions took effect on December 10, 2025. Platforms removed or restricted about 4.7 million accounts almost immediately. Yet eSafety's follow-up found that the share of surveyed 8–15-year-olds with an account on at least one restricted platform fell from 49.7% to 31.3%, not to zero. 

Among parents whose child still had an account, 66.8% said the platform had not asked the child to verify their age; 23.3% reported their child had bypassed an age check, and 10.3% said their child opened another account after deactivation.

There is another issue we should discuss separately from social media: children being drawn into political mobilisation.

At the July Jantar Mantar protests, reporters found Class 8 and Class 9 students among the demonstrators. One 14-year-old told India Today he had little connection to the protest's main demand. Another protester, who later said she was 15, was named in a Zero FIR over abusive slogans against the Prime Minister and subsequently appeared in a video saying she had been influenced by people around her. India Today noted that it could not independently verify her claimed age.

This concern is not confined to one movement or one party. NCPCR has previously sought police action after videos showed children raising violent slogans during a political protest, saying they appeared to have been used as political tools. 

In July 2026, Odisha's child-rights commission also issued notices over schoolchildren participating in a political rally during school hours.

Children can have opinions. Teenagers can care deeply about public issues. But there is an important difference between genuine youth participation and adults organising, coaching or exploiting minors for political theatre.

And once a protest crowd becomes chaotic or violent, the person exposed to the consequences may be a 14- or 15-year-old.

That child-safety standard should be applied consistently, regardless of the political party, ideology or cause involved.

body:
OCR of Tavleen Singh article "Democracy at work or disaster":

IN TIMES OF trouble, the worst thing a government can do is respond with arrogance and disdain. Narendra Modi is among the most skilled and sophisticated political leaders I have ever met, but this is one lesson he appears not to have learned. So, when this newspaper published its excellent investigation into the Election Commission last week, his response was to deploy his most articulate spokesmen onto TV chat shows and social media platforms to fight back hard. They did, but in the stupidest, most arrogant way.

With smug expressions and fake smiles pasted on their faces, they repeated ad nauseum that serious disagreements among the three election commissioners were a sign that India was a vibrant democracy. A puzzling and farcical viewpoint. But afterwards the ones who are always too clever by half changed tactics and as usual blamed the Congress Party. They recounted how many times election commissioners had been controlled by the government in Congress times. Names such as Naveen Chawla and MS Gill were brought up to prove this. One was a family friend of the Gandhis and the other had been rewarded with a seat in the Rajya Sabha and made a minister after he retired from the Election Commission. True.

It is also true that elections in Kashmir were openly rigged for decades. But does that justify what has been done now in the name of the Special Intensive Revision or SIR to give it the acronym that has gained a notoriety that strikes dread in the hearts of those whose election credentials it seeks to revise? Shashi Tharoor wrote a detailed and disturbing piece in this newspaper last week so I am not going to go into the numbers of voters who have been deleted wrongly. What I learned from it was that half the Delhi voters had been deleted. And in West Bengal nearly all those who had appealed against being deleted had found their voting rights restored after appealing to tribunals but by then the election was over.

There have been doubts about this SIR for months as there have been about the integrity of the election process itself. Rahul Gandhi has led the charge and in Bihar tried to make vote chori the fulcrum of his campaign. I have been among those who doubted the charges because I continue to believe that no matter how much tampering happens and it does it usually does not change the result of an election. Besides if you have been in journalism for as long as I have it is hard to forget how bad things used to be. Especially in rural India.

I remember ballot boxes being stolen by mafia types. I remember lower caste voters being forced to vote with a gun pointed at them by rural thugs. One reason so many criminals ended up in Parliament and our legislative assemblies is because these mafias discovered that if they could win elections for others they might as well start winning for themselves. In the process they discovered that there was more money to be made from serving the people than from crime. Indian democracy has been deeply damaged because of this.

So what happens now that Gyanesh Kumar has become the villain of a very ugly story? If I were him thankfully I am not I would gracefully exit the stage after declaring with a pained expression on my face that I have done no wrong but am happy to resign until a commission of inquiry establishes my innocence. Who knows but he may have done this by the time you read this piece which would be good for him. But the damage done to the Modi government still needs repair.

It needs to prove to the Indian people that it has not been trying to steal elections by disqualifying voters who do not vote BJP and by conducting an SIR that now has a huge cloud hanging over it. Instead of ordering its supporters and social media trolls to bang on about toolkits and foreign money it should spend some time introspecting about why so many things are starting to go so wrong. Why is Modi these days appearing to be constantly misreading the political mood? When the Cockroach Janta Party descended on Jantar Mantar there was such mishandling that shooting at students with pellet guns became more important than paper leaks. Then came the disastrous handling of Modis birthday celebrations. The acres of diyas of blessing that were lit brought shame to the birthday boy when small children were seen collecting oil from diyas to take home for their families.

The latest mishandling has been the way his government responded to The Indian Express story. BJP spokesmen were seen openly defending Gyanesh Kumar on TV and social media without anyone noticing that in doing this they were proving the opposition parties charge that the Election Commission had become a tool of the government. With so many things going so wrong the Prime Minister needs to conduct a special intensive revision of his team if he wants to regain a measure of lost credibility. And if he has not already asked Gyanesh Kumar to do so because he has become a major liability for the government. Besides it can be said with certainty that he has lost the trust of voters.

body:
WHEN THE ELECTION COMMISSION ITSELF IS UNDER QUESTION

https://t.co/8MLxqS84oz

THE QUESTIONS ARE NO LONGER COMING ONLY FROM THE OPPOSITION.

The Indian Express investigation reported that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi recorded objections at least 14 times in 10 months over decisions relating to electoral rolls, SIR and the Commission's IT systems. 

Now the controversy has moved beyond the walls of the Election Commission.

CEC Gyanesh Kumar's youth-awareness programmes in Meerut and Varanasi were postponed. The ECI says the postponements were routine and unrelated to the internal controversy, citing logistical and scheduling reasons. 

At the same time, NDA ally Chirag Paswan publicly said that if questions are being raised about the Election Commission, the Commission must answer the public and remove doubts about the electoral process. 

And on September 25, Delhi Police dispersed protesters at Jantar Mantar; Newslaundry reported that journalist Irfan Ahmed was detained and that his microphone was allegedly snatched and thrown away. 

This is the point where every democrat should stop and ask:

Why is there so much institutional controversy around something as fundamental as the electoral roll?

We don't need conspiracy theories.
We don't need unverified accusations.
We need records, explanations, transparency and accountability.

If objections were formally recorded, answer them.
If the objections were resolved, publish how.
If the electoral database is functioning properly, make its safeguards transparent.
If programmes were postponed for ordinary reasons, explain those reasons clearly.

Because the legitimacy of every elected government ultimately rests on one simple principle:

The citizen must be able to trust that their vote exists, is counted, and cannot be arbitrarily denied.

Democracy survives not when citizens blindly trust institutions —
but when institutions are strong enough to withstand scrutiny.

Advocate Vrinda Grover informs, "The honourable Supreme Court of India has today passed a very significant order. As we know that from 20th to 25th July, there were very active protests in Delhi, at Jantar Mantar and in many parts of the country relating to reform in education. During the protests, police across states have launched cases, criminal cases against the protesters, against the youth. There is now an assurance that was given on 25th July by the Union government to the Cockroach Janta Party representatives that they will not pursue any of the criminal proceedings and they will give compensation. In so far as the innumerable FIRs launched across states, from Bihar to West Bengal, UP, Madhya Pradesh, Assam, Delhi, of course. All those FIRs today, by the order of the honourable Supreme Court, and with the applications were moved by the states. So the states and the Union government have said that they will not pursue, they are to be quashed and the court has passed an order quashing the FIRs, all the FIRs. The Supreme Court has invoked its extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 142 of the Constitution of India because the court says the right to protest, the freedom to protest and express yourself is a fundamental right and that cannot be taken away. What is also significant is that with regards to the compensation they have agreed that it will be formulated and paid in the next three months..."
